messages.content:
You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:

CREATE TABLE museum (
    Museum_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Num_of_Staff INT,
    Open_Year TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Museum_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE visitor (
    ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Level_of_membership INT,
    Age INT,
    UNIQUE (ID)
);

CREATE TABLE visit (
    Museum_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    visitor_ID TEXT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Num_of_Ticket INT,
    Total_spent REAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Museum_ID, visitor_ID),
    UNIQUE (Museum_ID, visitor_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (visitor_ID) REFERENCES visitor(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Museum_ID) REFERENCES museum(Museum_ID)
);

When you have a final SQL query to present, always wrap it in a sql markdown code fence like this:

```sql
SELECT ...
```

This makes it easy to identify your answer. Only use one ```sql fence for your final query.

If you mean visitors who have visited the most museums, this query will rank them by number of museum visits:

```sql
SELECT
    v.ID,
    v.Name,
    COUNT(vi.Museum_ID) AS total_museums_visited
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
GROUP BY v.ID, v.Name
ORDER BY total_museums_visited DESC, v.Name;
```

If you want “frequent” to mean something else, like visitors who bought the most tickets or spent the most money, I can adjust it.
I want to focus on visitors who have been to these museums more than once.

Since the schema only allows one row per visitor–museum pair, I’m assuming “been to these museums more than once” means they have `Num_of_Ticket > 1` for that museum.

```sql
SELECT
    v.ID,
    v.Name AS Visitor_Name,
    m.Museum_ID,
    m.Name AS Museum_Name,
    vi.Num_of_Ticket,
    vi.Total_spent
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
JOIN museum AS m
    ON m.Museum_ID = vi.Museum_ID
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
ORDER BY vi.Num_of_Ticket DESC, v.Name, m.Name;
```

If you want, I can also rewrite this to show only the visitors, ranked by how many museums they’ve revisited.
I need to focus on visitors who have gone to those museums.

If you want to focus on the visitors only, and include those who went to a museum more than once, you can group by visitor:

```sql
SELECT
    v.ID,
    v.Name,
    COUNT(*) AS museums_visited_more_than_once
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
GROUP BY v.ID, v.Name
ORDER BY museums_visited_more_than_once DESC, v.Name;
```

This returns each visitor who has visited at least one museum more than once, along with how many such museums they revisited.
I just need the unique IDs of these visitors who have gone to those museums.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT vi.visitor_ID
FROM visit AS vi
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
ORDER BY vi.visitor_ID;
```
I also need the names of these visitors along with their IDs.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT
    v.ID,
    v.Name
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
ORDER BY v.ID;
```
I need to get the ages of these visitors along with their names too.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT
    v.ID,
    v.Name,
    v.Age
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
ORDER BY v.ID;
```
I want to focus on visitors specifically to museums.

If you want each qualifying visitor tied to the specific museum(s) they visited more than once, use:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT
    v.ID,
    v.Name,
    v.Age,
    m.Museum_ID,
    m.Name AS Museum_Name
FROM visitor AS v
JOIN visit AS vi
    ON v.ID = vi.visitor_ID
JOIN museum AS m
    ON vi.Museum_ID = m.Museum_ID
WHERE vi.Num_of_Ticket > 1
ORDER BY v.ID, m.Museum_ID;
```
